newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: American Football - Plenty of support assured for the "Fighting Irish'.
newsitem.headline: American Football - Plenty of support assured for the "Fighting Irish'.

text.p: The "Fighting Irish' of the University of Notre Dame are assured plenty of home support when they take on the U.S. Navy Academy in an American football classic at Croke Park on Saturday (start 1300 GMT).
"I'd imagine most of the crowd will be for us because of our nickname, the cap, the Catholic link and the Irish-American studies programme we run," Notre Dame team coach Lou Holtz said.
"But by the same token, a lot of Irish people would have had relatives serve in the Navy. It's still an away game for us," he added.
The University of Notre Dame was founded by a French missionary, Edward Sorin, in the early 1840's.
Its identity was cemented by the wave of predominantly Catholic European immigrants who arrived in the United States in the second-half of the 19th century.

The legend of the "Fighting Irish' was created when Norwegian-born coach, Knute Rockne, took the University team all over the United States in the 1920's to take on all-comers, including sides representing both the Army and the Navy.
Under Rockne, Notre Dame remained unbeaten for five seasons and won the 1925 national championship. He was killed in a car carsh in 1931.
Uncertainty surrounds the origins of the nickname "Fighting Irish', which was popularised in the 1920's by Frank Wallace in his New York Daily News columns.

One story has it that the nickname stuck after Northwestern supporters chanted "Kill the Fighting Irish, Kill the Fighting Irish" at the interval during a 1899 game. Notre Dame were leading 5-0 at the time.
Another has it that at half-time in a game against Michigan one angry Notre Dame supporter called out to the team: "What's wrong with you. Are we the fighting Irish or are we not?"
A third story, which appeared in the 1929 Notre Dame Scholastic, has it that the term was an "unkind appelation" -- ill-gained when the team travelled for away games.
"The term, while given in irony, has become our heritage," the Scholastic said.
The Leprechaun, which appears on the team helmet, has long been officially registered as the University logo.

Since he took over in 1985, current team coach Lou Holtz has led the side to 95 wins and to the 1988 national championship. The team has experienced mixed fortunes so far this season, winning only two of their opening six games.

The Navy Academy, who have not beaten Notre Dame since 1963, go into the game in good form having won five of their opening six matches this season under coach Charlie Weatherbie. This is their best start to a season since the 1970's.
Navy's explosive offence (attack) has averaged 45 points in the last four games and among their scalps this year are Air Force, who beat Notre Dame a fortnight ago.
But the "Midshipmen' preparations for Saturday's game took a knock when Bill the goat, the team mascot, was not allowed travel to Ireland because of the quarantine laws.
Saturday's game will involve two huge squads of offensive and defensive players but both teams are only allowed field 11 players at the one time.
The game will be split into four quarters with each quarter lasting for 15 minutes of playing time. The event is expected to last between three and four hours in total.
